rhs_question_text: A small bakery uses a spreadsheet to calculate its weekly staff wages. Give one benefit of using formulas rather than completing each wage calculation by hand. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Copying a tested formula recalculates many wages automatically when hours or rates change; this reduces repeated manual calculation and errors.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for a concrete, developed spreadsheet advantage such as automatic recalculation, applying a copied formula, improved accuracy or what-if analysis. Bare 'faster' needs explanation.

rhs_question_text: The bakery already uses a spreadsheet. Name TWO other TYPES of application software suitable for this business. For each type, give one distinct task the bakery could complete with it. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Examples: DBMS to maintain customer/supplier records; word processor for employment letters; DTP for menus; graphics editor for adverts; presentation software for staff training. No brand required.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Two marks per suitable software type + business-specific task; no spreadsheet (given); don't award a standalone brand name as software type.

rhs_question_text: The bakery uses paid closed-source software to manage ingredients. Describe three possible drawbacks to the business of choosing closed-source software rather than open-source software. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: The business may need licences or subscription fees; cannot inspect/change the proprietary source itself; cannot fix a bug or add specialised features without the vendor; may become dependent on vendor updates/support.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per different drawback, max three. Do not merely list the advantages of open source in reverse without a closed-source consequence.

rhs_question_text:
A museum opens its interactive kiosk each morning. For each statement about its BIOS/UEFI-style startup firmware, write TRUE or FALSE. [3]
1. It normally carries out initial hardware tests or setup before launching the OS.
2. Its essential boot instructions must be downloaded afresh from the internet every time power is turned on.
3. It can initiate the process of locating and loading the operating system.
rhs_answer_points_draft: 1 True; 2 False; 3 True.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per correctly evaluated statement; max three. This is a newly authored RHS three-row table, not the OCR statement list.

rhs_question_text: A chain of pharmacies backs up the files from several branches into remote virtual storage. Explain two different reasons this is useful for backups rather than relying only on a drive at each branch. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Remote backup copies may survive a fire/flood at a branch; capacity can be expanded and files can be retrieved from other branches; many devices' backup can be centralised.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each distinct backup-related benefit. Generic statements such as 'lots of space' without development are insufficient.

rhs_question_text: A sports centre connects its office, reception and finance computers to one local area network. State three different benefits of this arrangement. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Examples: share printers; share permitted files; centralised access permissions/security; common internet connection; central backups; easier support and software updates.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each different, practical LAN benefit, maximum three.

rhs_question_text: The sports centre uses different makes of network equipment. Explain what a network protocol is and how it enables information to be exchanged. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: An agreed collection of rules about communication/data transfer (format, order, error handling); devices following those rules can successfully send and receive data.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for a set of communication rules and one for governing successful data transmission. 'A rule' alone is insufficient.

rhs_question_text: Give the names of TWO different protocols that may be used when computers communicate on the sports-centre LAN. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Examples: TCP, IP, DHCP, HTTPS, HTTP, Ethernet, FTP or SMTP where applicable.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per different valid protocol. Versions of the same protocol (IPv4 and IPv6) do not count as two different protocols.

rhs_question_text: The sports centre's network protocols are arranged in layers. Explain three benefits of layering rather than designing a single monolithic protocol. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Each layer has a defined task; a layer hides implementation details from others; developers can change/test one layer without rewriting the whole system; separate standards aid interoperability and fault isolation.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per distinct reason for protocol layering, maximum three. Repetition of 'easier' without explaining the specific benefit is not enough.

rhs_question_text: A factory uses a computer to activate an emergency shut-off before a strict deadline. Identify the most appropriate TYPE of operating system for this task. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Real-time operating system (RTOS).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for real-time operating system; it has a bounded-response requirement.

rhs_question_text: A college currently uses a real-time OS in one laboratory machine. Name THREE other types of operating system and, for each type, explain a characteristic that distinguishes it. [6]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Multitasking: enables multiple applications to make progress in the same period. Multi-user: permits multiple people to use computing resources concurrently. Distributed: coordinates multiple networked computers as one task/system. Embedded: designed for restricted dedicated functions.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Three name-and-correct-feature pairs, 2 marks each. Real-time is already given; simply having several user accounts does not define multi-user concurrency.

rhs_question_text: A school server receives an interrupt while another program runs. Explain three stages of how the processor and operating system might service the interrupt and continue the original program. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: The CPU detects/accepts the interrupt (subject to priority), saves relevant registers/state, loads and executes the interrupt service routine (ISR), then restores the earlier state and resumes.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Three different accurate stages, maximum three; references to priority, ISR address and state restoration are relevant.

rhs_question_text: A community library uses one shared computer for cataloguing, web access and public bookings. Discuss how an operating system manages and protects RAM so these applications can coexist. Include allocation, virtual memory, paging or segmentation, and the consequences of poor memory management. Evaluate which challenges matter most to the library. [9]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Consider allocating and freeing memory, preventing one process accessing another's memory, fixed-size paging versus variable-size segments, fragmentation trade-offs and secondary-storage-backed virtual memory. Excessive swapping can cause major slowdown/thrashing; efficient management protects data and keeps essential public services responsive.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Holistic nine-mark teacher assessment: 7–9 detailed, applied and balanced evaluation; 4–6 sound with some application; 1–3 basic relevant points; zero no credit. Do not score by nine isolated keywords.

rhs_question_text:
A community coding club writes a reverse-polish (postfix) calculator using a stack called numbers. Entered integers are pushed. The command + removes the top two items, adds them and pushes their sum. The command - removes the top two items, subtracts the first removed from the second and pushes that result. The command ! removes the top item, prints it and stops. A command cannot pop from an empty stack.
Fill all five blanks in this original calculator routine. [5]
repeat
  token = input("Value or command:")
  if token == ______ then
    print(numbers.pop())
  elseif token == "+" or token == ______ then
    last = numbers.pop()
    first = numbers.pop()
    if token == "+" then
      numbers.push(____________)
    else
      numbers.push(first - last)
    endif
  else
    numbers.push(____________)
  endif
until token == ______
rhs_answer_points_draft: The blanks are: "!"; "-"; first + last; token; "!".
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each correctly completed blank in the correct location, max five. Arithmetic order matters for subtraction.

rhs_question_text:
A community coding club writes a reverse-polish (postfix) calculator using a stack called numbers. Entered integers are pushed. The command + removes the top two items, adds them and pushes their sum. The command - removes the top two items, subtracts the first removed from the second and pushes that result. The command ! removes the top item, prints it and stops. A command cannot pop from an empty stack.
Write the full occupied stack (bottom → top) after each input in this sequence: 8, 7, +, 6. [3]
The first state after 8 is given: [8]. Record the remaining three states.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each complete correct subsequent stack state, max three; include order.

rhs_question_text:
A community coding club writes a reverse-polish (postfix) calculator using a stack called numbers. Entered integers are pushed. The command + removes the top two items, adds them and pushes their sum. The command - removes the top two items, subtracts the first removed from the second and pushes that result. The command ! removes the top item, prints it and stops. A command cannot pop from an empty stack.
For each independent input sequence, give the single value printed by the calculator. [3]
(a) 9, 3, +, !
(b) 10, 5, +, 8, -, !
(c) 25, 5, -, 2, 3, +, -, !
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per exact printed result, max three.

rhs_question_text:
A community coding club writes a reverse-polish (postfix) calculator using a stack called numbers. Entered integers are pushed. The command + removes the top two items, adds them and pushes their sum. The command - removes the top two items, subtracts the first removed from the second and pushes that result. The command ! removes the top item, prints it and stops. A command cannot pop from an empty stack.
The user enters 4, 2, -, +, ! and the routine fails. Explain the failure and why the order of the tokens causes it. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: After 4,2,- the stack holds [2]. The next + attempts to pop two values, but only one remains, causing stack underflow; the algorithm has no empty/size check before the second pop.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for identifying the insufficient operands, one for the actual pop/underflow failure, one for relating it to absent size validation.

rhs_question_text: A music-streaming service stores pending song requests. Compare the removal order of a stack with that of a queue, making clear which item comes out first in each structure. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: A stack is LIFO (the newest item comes out first), while a queue is FIFO (the oldest item comes out first).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for LIFO and one for FIFO, with matching explanation.

rhs_question_text: A programmer has an array and a list. Describe two relevant differences between them in typical programming languages. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: An array is usually fixed-size/contiguous and accessed by numeric index; a dynamic list can change length and may provide insertion/removal methods. Both can be indexed in some languages, so indexing alone is not a universal difference.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Up to two accurate, distinct contrasts, avoiding claims about universal language implementations.

rhs_question_text: State one difference between an immutable tuple and a mutable list. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: A tuple's contents/structure cannot be modified after creation; a mutable list can be changed.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for the immutability difference.

rhs_question_text: A museum represents a sequence of objects as a singly linked list. Explain how it follows pointers to access the second node's stored value. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Start at the list's head pointer to locate the first node, read that node's next reference/pointer, and follow it to the second node before reading its data; the pointer may be null if a second node does not exist.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for head, one for reading the next-pointer of the first node, one for following it to the second node/data (and handling end-of-list if mentioned).

rhs_question_text: An aquarium's ticket machine assigns the denary ID 189 to a visitor. Convert 189 into hexadecimal. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: BD.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for BD; exact source number and hexadecimal result preserved.

rhs_question_text: A sensor stores the unsigned binary word 1010101111. Express it in hexadecimal, retaining all digits. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: 2AF.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for 2AF.

rhs_question_text: Represent the signed denary number −107 in eight-bit sign-and-magnitude format. [1]
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for sign bit 1 and seven-bit magnitude 1101011, giving 11101011.

rhs_question_text: Represent the signed denary number −107 in eight-bit two's complement format. [1]
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for the exact eight-bit two's complement of −107.

rhs_question_text: Give one advantage of using two's complement rather than sign-and-magnitude for storing negative integers. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Two's complement has a single zero and permits ordinary binary addition/subtraction with the same adder; it also provides an extra representable negative value.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One valid specific advantage; max one.

rhs_question_text: A tide-modelling computer needs to store −15.75 in normalised two's-complement floating point. Use exactly EIGHT mantissa bits and FOUR exponent bits, with the binary point immediately after the mantissa sign bit. Show your conversion and both bit fields. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: −15.75 = −0.984375 × 2^4. Eight-bit signed fractional mantissa = 10000010; four-bit exponent +4 = 0100. Thus 10000010 0100.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Four teaching points: signed binary representation, normalising by 4 places, full mantissa 10000010, exponent 0100. Full correct fields plus valid working may earn all four.

rhs_question_text: A controller reads a normalised floating-point bit pattern with a four-bit two's-complement mantissa 0100 and a four-bit two's-complement exponent 1110. The binary point is after the sign bit. Convert its value to denary, showing your working. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: 0100 as signed fraction is +0.5; 1110 represents exponent −2; 0.5 × 2^−2 = 0.125.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for exponent −2, one for correct mantissa/binary-shift working, one for 0.125.

rhs_question_text: Complete these two statements about a binary floating-point storage format: (i) more mantissa bits generally increase the ______ of representable numbers; (ii) more exponent bits generally increase their ______. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: (i) precision/accuracy; (ii) range/magnitude.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One correct concept per blank, max two.

rhs_question_text: An engineer is deciding whether to write a microcontroller program in assembly or a high-level language. Describe TWO distinct differences, giving both sides of each contrast. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Assembly uses processor mnemonics and an assembler, often with roughly one-to-one machine instructions and hardware specificity. A high-level language uses more abstract instructions, compiler/interpreter translation and is generally more portable; many machine instructions may implement one high-level statement.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Two paired same-feature comparisons, up to two marks per pair. Unpaired lists cannot earn the full four.

rhs_question_text: A drone controller has four CPU cores. Give one condition under which those cores can make part of its application execute more quickly. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: The program has independent instructions/threads that can execute concurrently on different cores.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for simultaneous execution of independent instructions/threads, rather than a bare 'more programs'.

rhs_question_text: A game has been moved from a single-core computer to a multicore computer, but one stage still takes the same time. Explain two possible reasons why the extra cores have not helped this stage. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: The stage has instructions dependent on previous results and cannot be parallelised; software may be single-threaded; other bottlenecks such as memory/cache speed may limit performance.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Up to two distinct relevant reasons, including inability to execute dependent instructions in parallel.

rhs_question_text: A rescue robot sends messages to its base station over Wi-Fi and saves operator passwords and mission reports locally. Evaluate when encryption and when hashing should be used. Compare symmetric and asymmetric encryption, explain how password checking differs from storing reversible files, and assess trade-offs for the robot. [9]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key and is efficient for protecting data/files; asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair, supporting secure key exchange or identity verification. Hash functions map data to fixed-size digests and are not reversible encryption; passwords should be stored with suitable salted password hashing, while private reports needing recovery should be encrypted. Transport encryption protects intercepted messages; keyed hashes/MACs or digital signatures can aid integrity/authenticity. Discuss key protection, resource needs, threats and fit to the robot.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Nine-mark holistic teacher marking: thorough balanced applied discussion 7–9; sound but limited 4–6; basic 1–3; none 0. This is a teacher-authored synopsis, not official band wording.

rhs_question_text:
A school's river-monitoring club is creating its own web page. Fill five blanks in the HTML listing below so it contains a bulleted list, a link, a login label and a form with a password entry and submit control. [5]

River sensor centre

____
  • Track river levels
  • Send alerts
    • Current status

    ____

    Code:
rhs_answer_points_draft: Blanks, in order: <ul>; href; Login; password; submit.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per correct HTML blank, maximum five. In this independent version the secret field intentionally uses input type=password. Case-insensitive element spelling accepted where valid.

rhs_question_text: A community river-monitoring website uses an HTML h1 heading for its main title. Write a CSS rule that makes the h1 text WHITE and gives it a RED background. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: h1 { color: white; background-color: red; }
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for h1 selector and braces, one for white foreground, one for red background; equivalent CSS hex colour values accepted.

rhs_question_text: A student takes original photos for a club's website. Give the FULL name of the UK Act that protects the copyright in original photographs, and explain TWO consequences or rights it provides to their creator. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. Protection arises automatically; the copyright holder controls copying and licensing of protected work; unlicensed copying may give rise to legal remedies.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for the full Act name and up to two for ownership, automatic protection and permission/licensing consequences. Check current law before deployment.

rhs_question_text: A pupil wants to add another photographer's image to a public school project. Describe TWO separate lawful ways to obtain an appropriate right to use it. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Obtain a suitable licence or explicit permission from the copyright holder; purchase a usage licence; use openly licensed imagery under the applicable Creative Commons terms; use public-domain images with checked status.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per valid specific route to lawful use. An unqualified 'ask permission' without identifying the owner is insufficient.

rhs_question_text: A sailing club keeps activity logs in TblSessionLog(ID, UserType, DateAccessed). It wants to remove only records whose UserType is the string "Archived". Write a complete SQL DELETE command with the correct WHERE condition. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: DELETE FROM TblSessionLog WHERE UserType = "Archived";
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for DELETE FROM TblSessionLog, one for correctly quoted WHERE UserType = "Archived". Do not use DELETE * or ==.

rhs_question_text: State TWO requirements of a database table being in First Normal Form. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Atomic single-valued fields (no repeating lists in one cell); each attribute has a unique name; records can be uniquely identified by a key; no repeating attribute groups.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each of two different valid 1NF requirements; general redundancy alone is not sufficient.

rhs_question_text: A sailing club has a field DateAccessed containing "2023-06-01, 2023-06-02" inside a single record cell. Explain why this particular field prevents the table from being in First Normal Form. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: DateAccessed holds multiple dates as a list within one cell. Its contents are not atomic and should be separated into individual records or an appropriate linked table.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for identifying the problem field, one for explaining multiple values/non-atomic field content.

The cycling club's digitCheck(n) function sums all the decimal digits of a positive integer n and returns that sum MOD 10.
What does digitCheck(3178) return? [1]
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for 9.

rhs_question_text:
The cycling club's digitCheck(n) function sums all the decimal digits of a positive integer n and returns that sum MOD 10.
Write an algorithm to input a positive integer and then save the original number and result of digitCheck() on two separate lines in a file named clubchecks.txt. Open for writing and close the file. [5]
rhs_answer_points_draft:
number = int(input("Number:"))
check = digitCheck(number)
f = openWrite("clubchecks.txt")
f.writeLine(number)
f.writeLine(check)
f.close()
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Five separate criteria: input and store integer (1), call digitCheck with integer (1), open/close the correct file (1), write input (1), write check value (1).

rhs_question_text: An original greenhouse alarm has inputs A, B, C. A and B feed OR, its result is inverted, and the output is XORed with C to create F. Derive the Boolean expression. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: F = NOT(A OR B) XOR C.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Mark one for grouped NOT of OR(A,B) and one for XOR C.

For the greenhouse circuit F = NOT(A OR B) XOR C, complete the output column. [3]
A | B | C | F
0 | 0 | 0 | ?
0 | 0 | 1 | ?
0 | 1 | 0 | ?

rhs_question_text:
An RHS flood alarm uses this independently designed 4-variable Karnaugh map. AB rows and CD columns use Gray-code order:
AB / CD | 00 | 01 | 11 | 10
00 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0
01 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0
11 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1
10 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1
Circle the largest valid adjacent groups of 1s and write a minimal sum-of-products Boolean expression. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: F = (NOT A AND NOT C) OR (A AND NOT D). One group where A=0 and C=0; another where A=1 and D=0.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for valid group selection, one each for the two accurate terms, one for their OR relationship (dependent on both terms).

rhs_question_text: A city council is considering wider investigatory powers to monitor communications in serious-crime investigations. Residents want safeguards for lawful private activities. Discuss advantages, drawbacks and safeguards of legally authorised surveillance and interception, referring to the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 and later legislation. Justify your view. [12]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Discuss possible detection and evidence-gathering benefits against privacy, intrusion, misuse, data security and chilling effects. Assess necessity, proportionality, independent authorisation, oversight and redress. Current law must be separately reviewed before classroom use.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Teacher marked 12-mark levels-of-response, not 12 isolated points. Basic 1–4; sound and applied 5–8; thorough balanced conclusion 9–12; 0 none.
